research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. What `SSLContext` governs, and what the reported value refers to

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents an implementation of a secure-socket protocol and acts as a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances. It is initialized with optional key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source. The context also holds state shared by objects created under it, including TLS session state.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The reported finding refers to the **first argument** of:

```text
SSLContext.init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)
```

The API documents `km` as “the sources of authentication keys,” while `tm` supplies peer-authentication trust decisions. A `KeyManager` chooses the local authentication credentials to send; a `TrustManager` determines whether remote credentials and the connection are trusted. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The wording “was not observed coming from a `KeyManagerFactory`” is therefore a **static provenance claim about the `KeyManager[]` value passed as `km`**, not a documented SSL/TLS handshake result, negotiated-protocol result, certificate-validation result, or hostname-verification result. The cited CrySL file contains the predicate `generatedKeyManagers[km]`; it does **not** itself contain the text `KeyManagerFactory` or define how that predicate is established.  
Rule source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

In particular, this predicate should not be read as evidence about the enabled or negotiated TLS version. The JSSE guide states that an `SSLContext` acquired for one protocol may implement additional protocols, while protocol lists allowed for a connection are represented by `SSLParameters`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

---

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation

#### Documented API usage

The Java API permits these `SSLContext.init` inputs:

* A `KeyManager[]` as the source of local authentication keys.
* A `TrustManager[]` as the source of peer-trust decisions.
* A `SecureRandom` source.
* `null` for either manager array, in which case installed security providers are searched for the highest-priority appropriate factory; `null` for the random source uses a default implementation. Only the first manager of a particular implementation type in each array is used.  
  Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The JSSE Reference Guide expressly documents two ways to create `KeyManager` objects:

1. obtain them from `KeyManagerFactory`; **or**
2. provide a concrete implementation of the `KeyManager` interface.

Thus, the official documentation does **not** require every `KeyManager[]` passed to `SSLContext.init` to originate from `KeyManagerFactory`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

Where factory-based key material management is appropriate, the documented factory sequence is: initialize a `KeyManagerFactory` with a `KeyStore` and password, or provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters`, then obtain the `KeyManager[]` through `getKeyManagers()`. The factory documentation describes it as producing one key manager per type of key material.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))

#### Safe-use points documented by JSSE

A `KeyManager` handles local credential selection; it is not the component that decides whether a remote peer is trusted. That role belongs to a `TrustManager`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

For raw `SSLSocket` or `SSLEngine` use, the JSSE guide says peer credentials should be checked before data is sent. It further documents `SSLParameters.setEndpointIdentificationAlgorithm`, whose nonempty setting requires endpoint-identification processing during the TLS/DTLS handshake.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

#### Official remediation for “not from `KeyManagerFactory`”

There is **no official JDK API statement** that treats a concrete/custom `KeyManager` as incorrect, nor is there an official `SSLContext` remediation specifically for a static-analysis finding that a manager array was not observed as factory-produced. The documented `KeyManagerFactory` route is an available supported construction route, but it is not stated as a mandatory replacement for custom `KeyManager` implementations. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))

Accordingly, a requirement to prove `KeyManagerFactory` provenance comes from the CrySL predicate/detector policy, rather than from the `SSLContext.init` API contract.

---

### 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and documented migration

#### Persisted formats

The `SSLContext.init` documentation defines in-memory initialization inputs; it specifies no persisted `SSLContext` format and no serialized `KeyManager[]` format. `KeyManagerFactory.init(KeyStore, char[])` identifies a `KeyStore` as a typical source of key material, but does not define a conversion or migration format between a custom `KeyManager` and a factory-produced one. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Therefore, the official sources reviewed provide **no documented persisted-data migration path** for changing the origin of the `KeyManager[]`.

#### Wire format and TLS compatibility

The sources do not document a wire-format transformation caused merely by changing whether a `KeyManager[]` is custom or obtained through `KeyManagerFactory`. However, `KeyManager` selection affects the authentication credentials sent to the remote peer, so changing key material, credential-selection behavior, or associated provider behavior is not documented as wire-equivalent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

The CrySL rule separately constrains the requested `SSLContext` protocol string. That is distinct from enabled and negotiated protocols:

* `SSLContext.getInstance` obtains an implementation of the requested secure-socket protocol.
* The JSSE guide says a returned implementation may support other protocols as well.
* `SSLParameters` holds the list of protocols allowed for a connection. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Thus, neither `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` nor the CrySL literals `"TLSv1.2"`/`"TLSv1.3"` alone document the final negotiated TLS version.

If a separate change also moves an application to TLS 1.3, Oracle’s JDK 11 release notes identify compatibility considerations: TLS 1.3 has different close behavior, disallows DSA certificate authentication, uses different cipher suites, and changes some session-resumption/key-update behavior. Those are protocol-upgrade considerations, not a documented effect of factory provenance alone.  
Source: https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-relnote-issues.html ([oracle.com](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-relnote-issues.html?utm_source=openai))

#### Platform-version support

* `SSLContext` and `KeyManagerFactory` have existed since Java 1.4. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
* `SSLParameters.setEndpointIdentificationAlgorithm` is documented since Java 7. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html))
* Oracle states that JDK 11 includes TLS 1.3 and defines `TLSv1.3` as an `SSLContext` algorithm name. ([oracle.com](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-relnote-issues.html?utm_source=openai))
* In the current Java SE 25 API, every Java-platform implementation is required to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3` `SSLContext` protocols; support for additional protocols remains implementation/release dependent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

No official source reviewed provides a migration procedure that guarantees behavioral, provider, credential-selection, wire, or interoperability equivalence when changing a custom `KeyManager[]` construction path to a `KeyManagerFactory` path.

---

### 4. Exact CrySL source rule matching and conditions

**Source:**  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl

The source scopes the specification to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. It declares matching events for `getInstance`, `init`, and `createSSLEngine`, and a forbidden zero-argument `getDefault` event. The relevant clauses are, verbatim:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext

FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
	Engine := se1 | se2;

ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
CONSTRAINTS
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};

REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```
